Summary and Source: Argentina signed a U.S.-Argentina Agreement on Reciprocal Trade and Investment (ARTI), with the labor commitment finalized around Feb 5, 2026: Argentina committed to "adopt and implement a prohibition on the importation of goods produced by forced or compulsory labor," placing it in USTR's lower 10% tariff tier. This was directly verified against the USTR fact sheet. No domestic Argentine bill or implementing regulation has been found tabled yet -- this is a treaty-level commitment only, structurally the same situation as Jordan's Article 2.9 commitment, and is reclassified from "No" to "Partial" for consistency with that precedent. No Argentina-specific hearing testimony found in the July 7-9 hearing record. Source: USTR fact sheet, Nov 2025/Feb 2026; White & Case / Gibson Dunn (law firm summaries of USTR determination). Summary and Source: Trade Minister Don Farrell rejected USTR's finding, calling the tariffs "unjustified and inconsistent" with the US-Australia FTA and asserting Australia already has "world-leading" modern slavery legislation; Australia also submitted written comments to USTR ahead of the July hearings. On July 16, 2026, the federal government announced it intends to introduce reforms to the Modern Slavery Act 2018 centered on a new criminal "failure to prevent" modern slavery offence for companies with over AUD 100 million revenue; this remains an announcement of intent only -- no bill has been tabled in Parliament -- and it would in any case be a corporate-liability offence, not an import prohibition. STALE-SOURCE GUARD (re-confirmed this run): search results periodically surface a headline that the Australian Senate "passed" a forced-labour import bill. That refers to Senator Rex Patrick's 2021/2022 private senator's bill, which lapsed before the 2022 election and never became law. It must not be treated as a current or enacted measure. Source: HCAMag / SBS News, June 3, 2026; Baker McKenzie, July 2026; Walk Free, July 2026. USTR issued its FINAL Section 301 forced-labor determination on July 23, 2026 (Ambassador Greer, per direction of the President), confirming a final tariff of 12.5% for Australia, timed to replace the expiring Section 122 10% global surcharge. Source: USTR press release and White House presidential action, July 23, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: No (Modern Slavery Act 2018 is a reporting regime, not an import prohibition; the announced "failure to prevent" offence is unlegislated and corporate-liability in nature, and the 2021 Senate private member's bill lapsed)

Summary and Source: The Customs Management (Amendment) Bill 2026 (new section 208A) passed the House of Assembly alongside the 2026-2027 Budget. The Bahamas government's own legislation portal (laws.bahamas.gov.bs) lists the bill by name under "Tabled in House of Assembly," while its Acts-by-Year register for 2026 -- re-fetched and re-parsed directly on August 4, 2026, still current through Act No. 2026-0038 (Environmental Health Services (Amendment) Act) -- lists 18 enacted Acts with NO Customs Management amendment among them. That is affirmative evidence of non-enactment from the government's own record, now confirmed on three consecutive runs. NOTE on tooling: this register 403s or returns empty for some clients, and a failed fetch is NOT evidence of change -- it has to be retrieved successfully before any conclusion is drawn. NOTE for future runs: The Tribune (July 28, 2026) describes the Customs Management reforms as having been "passed" before end-June as part of the budget legislation, and Agriculture Minister Jomo Campbell said the Bahamas intends "to be the seventh" country to secure the 10% tier -- but "passed" there refers to the House stage already recorded, not to Senate passage or the Governor-General's assent, neither of which any source has ever named. Channels exhausted include Parliament and Senate records, the Official Gazette, bahamas.gov.bs and Bahamas Information Services, the Office of the Prime Minister, the Attorney-General's office, Bahamas Customs notices, ZNS, the Library of Congress Global Legal Monitor, a Higgs & Johnson budget advisory, and the main Bahamian outlets. Source: Government of The Bahamas legislation portal (tabled register and Acts-by-Year register, re-verified August 4, 2026); The Tribune (Bahamas), July 24, 27 and 28, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Partial (Customs Management (Amendment) Bill 2026, new s.208A -- listed on the Bahamas government legislation portal's tabled-in-House-of-Assembly register and passed by the House alongside the 2026-2027 Budget; the same portal's 2026 Acts-by-Year register, re-parsed August 4, 2026 and current through Act No. 2026-0038, contains no Customs Management amendment, i.e. affirmative evidence of non-enactment)

Summary and Source: Under a Feb 2026 US-Bangladesh Agreement on Reciprocal Trade, Bangladesh committed that it "shall adopt and implement a prohibition on the importation of goods mined, produced, or manufactured wholly or in part by convict labor or forced or compulsory labor," per the official USTR fact sheet, earning it the lower 10% tariff tier. Separately, Bangladesh's Parliament passed the Bangladesh Labour (Amendment) Act, 2026 on April 9, 2026, a domestic labor-rights reform (forced-labor prohibitions per ILO Convention 190, anti-blacklisting) -- but this is not itself a forced-labor goods import prohibition. No implementing import-ban law found yet, so this remains a treaty-level commitment only -- the same situation as Jordan's Article 2.9 commitment -- and is reclassified from "No" to "Partial" for consistency. Source: USTR Fact Sheet (US-Bangladesh ART), Feb 2026; Dhaka Tribune, June 3, 2026; ESG Institute Bangladesh, 2026. Source: USTR press release and White House presidential action, July 23, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Partial (US-Bangladesh Agreement on Reciprocal Trade: Bangladesh commits to prohibit forced-labor-produced imports; treaty-level commitment only, no domestic import-ban law enacted yet -- the April 2026 Labour Amendment Act addresses domestic labor rights, not imports; reclassified from No to Partial for consistency with Jordan's equivalent precedent)

Summary and Source: STATUS CHANGE this run, No to Partial -- a policy-consistency correction, not a new event. Brazil has had a formally tabled forced-labour import-ban bill since 2015: PL 2.799/2015 (Dep. Davidson Magalhaes), which with PL 3717/2015 and PL 5072/2016 attached would prohibit importing and trading goods made with child, forced or compulsory labour, provide for seizure and forfeiture, and require the government to publish a six-monthly list of implicated companies drawing on ILO data and court decisions. Verified directly against the Chamber of Deputies' own tramitacao record (dadosabertos.camara.leg.br, 76 recorded events): the Labour Committee approved the rapporteur's substitutive on September 15, 2025 -- which expanded the original cocoa-only text to all products -- the Economic Development Committee (CDE) approved its parecer on June 10, 2026, and the bill was received by the Constitution, Justice and Citizenship Committee (CCJC) on June 12, 2026, where it is awaiting designation of a rapporteur. It is not enacted and still requires CCJC and Senate passage. Under the standing policy a formally tabled but unenacted import-ban bill is Partial, so the prior "No" was inconsistent with the classification rule rather than with the facts. Two dating corrections recorded: the CDE approval was June 10, 2026, not "the week of July 13" as this row previously stated, and the widely syndicated "committee approves" article is the Chamber's own September 15, 2025 story about the Labour Committee, not a 2026 item. Separately, Brazil's government (gov.br/Secom) called USTR's conclusion "regrettable," citing its ILO-recognised record; and a distinct, unrelated 25% Section 301 tariff (digital trade, ethanol, deforestation, IP) took effect July 22, 2026, on top of which the 12.5% forced-labour tariff was confirmed July 23, 2026. Source: Camara dos Deputados open-data tramitacao record and Camara news, September 15, 2025; gov.br/Secom; USTR press release, July 23, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Partial (PL 2.799/2015, with PL 3717/2015 and PL 5072/2016 attached, would prohibit importing and trading goods made with child/forced labour; substitutive approved by the Labour Committee September 15, 2025 and by the Economic Development Committee June 10, 2026, received by the Constitution and Justice Committee June 12, 2026 awaiting a rapporteur; not enacted, still requires CCJC and Senate passage)

Summary and Source: MinCIT published a draft resolution on July 15, 2026 for the Foreign Trade Single Window to act on forced-labour-linked goods, but it was never finalized. DIAN stated on July 24 that it lacks legal competence to issue the regulation MinCIT requested; El Tiempo published a letter showing DIAN did not act in time, and industry body ANDI publicly blamed DIAN's inaction for Colombia landing at 12.5%. As of July 27 MinCIT was still "reiterating" its call to DIAN and MinHacienda to update customs rules, with no decree or resolution issued, no competence determination, and no presidential intervention identified -- the standoff is now into its second week. Source: El Tiempo, July 25 and 27, 2026; El Heraldo and El Pais (Colombia), July 24-25, 2026; Infobae.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Partial (MinCIT draft resolution published July 15, 2026, still unfinalized; DIAN maintains it lacks competence to regulate and MinCIT was still publicly reiterating its request as of July 27 -- inter-institutional standoff unresolved, no decree issued)

Summary and Source: President Abinader issued Decreto num. 502-26 on July 23, 2026 -- the day the 12.5% US tariff took effect -- establishing an administrative procedure empowering the Direccion General de Aduanas (DGA), coordinated with the Labor Ministry, Public Ministry, Industry and Commerce and Foreign Affairs, to identify, restrict and prohibit importation of merchandise produced wholly or partly with forced labor. The decree creates a public registry of prohibited products and lets DGA preventively retain or bar suspect goods including consignments already in transit or sitting at port, with re-export or destruction as remedies. DATE DISCREPANCY RESOLVED this run: at least one secondary outlet (Revista Mercado) dates the decree to June 23, 2026; the Presidency's own decree page for 502-26 carries 23 de Julio 2026, so the July 23 date recorded here is confirmed against the primary source and the June date is incorrect. The private sector has raised implementation concerns and commentators question enforcement capacity; no implementing regulation has been issued and no enforcement action has yet been identified. Source: Presidencia de la Republica Dominicana (primary, decree page re-verified August 3, 2026); Diario Libre, July 23 and 26, 2026; El Nuevo Diario.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (Decreto No. 502-26, issued July 23, 2026 -- date confirmed against the Presidency's own decree page; establishes a public registry of prohibited products and empowers customs (DGA) to preventively retain and bar forced-labor-linked merchandise, including goods already in transit or at port, with re-export or destruction as remedies)

Summary and Source: Ecuador holds the 10% tier on the basis of COMEX Resolution 005-2026, which created the inter-institutional technical team (ETITF, spanning the Production Ministry, customs authority SENAE and the Labour Ministry) to restrict imports of forced-labor-produced goods; USTR credits the measure but assesses enforcement as weak, and no enforcement action has been identified. Production Minister Luis Alberto Jaramillo reiterated at USA Trade Connect 2026 in Guayaquil (July 28) that Ecuador "complies with its commitments and controls." New detail this run: the separate US-Ecuador Reciprocal Trade Agreement signed March 13, 2026 is NOT yet in force -- it still requires Constitutional Court review and National Assembly approval -- and Ecuador has a 12-month window to stand up its compliance systems. Ecuador's Yes therefore rests on the enacted COMEX resolution, not the unratified RTA. Source: El Universo and Primicias, July 2026; Ministerio de Produccion.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (COMEX Resolution 005-2026 establishing the inter-institutional mechanism restricting forced-labor-linked imports; USTR assesses enforcement as weak. The separate US-Ecuador RTA signed March 13, 2026 is not yet in force -- it still requires Constitutional Court review and National Assembly approval)

Summary and Source: USTR credits the EU with an enacted prohibition but assesses enforcement as inadequate because Regulation (EU) 2024/3015 is not applicable until December 14, 2027. Article 3 verified directly from EUR-Lex: "Economic operators shall not place or make available on the Union market products that are made with forced labour, nor shall they export such products." The Regulation is marked "(Text with EEA relevance)," the basis for Norway's incorporation, and Article 2(1) defines forced labour by reference to ILO Convention No. 29. The Commission's implementation guidelines of June 26, 2026 (C(2026) 4386 final) -- covering case selection and prioritisation, evidence standards, border and online enforcement and voluntary due diligence -- are confirmed on the Commission's own initiative page, as is the accompanying Forced Labour Single Portal, which is now live. New this run: the Commission has scheduled implementation-readiness webinars beginning September 2026. All of this is guidance and preparation for a still-inapplicable regulation, so classification is unchanged. Source: EUR-Lex (primary text); European Commission initiative 16292 and C(2026) 4386 final, June 26, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (Regulation (EU) 2024/3015, Article 3 prohibition, in force but not applicable until December 14, 2027; Commission implementation guidelines adopted June 26, 2026 and Forced Labour Single Portal live)

Summary and Source: Guatemala's Acuerdo Ministerial 377-2026 (published July 6, 2026) secured it the 10% tier but is not yet in force -- it takes effect 30 business days after publication, i.e. approximately mid-August 2026. Its scope is narrower than early reporting implied: rather than a blanket product or origin prohibition, it bars imports from a specific list of foreign companies. New detail this run: MINTRAB has said it lacks capacity to conduct extraterritorial investigations and will therefore build that list from international-source information, via a 90-business-day interinstitutional process with the Economy and Foreign Affairs ministries; the list has not been published. The private sector has set out five conditions it wants met on implementation. Classification stays Yes because the instrument is formally published by the competent authority, which the standing policy treats as enactment even before effectiveness. Source: Prensa Libre, July 27 and 30, 2026; La Hora; Diario de Centro America.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (Acuerdo Ministerial 377-2026, published July 6, 2026; NOT yet in force as of July 30, 2026 -- effective 30 business days after publication, ~mid-August 2026; scope limited to imports from a company-specific list which MINTRAB has not yet published)

Summary and Source: Honduras testified at the July 7 USTR hearing (Melvin Redondo, Presidential Office of Foreign Trade), announcing an executive decree creating an express legal prohibition on importing forced-labor-made goods with three enforcement mechanisms (importer declarations, a Ministry of Labour risk list, and binding customs opinions), and requested a 10% "bridge rate" pending completion of its own Reciprocal Trade Agreement. Honduras's Council of Ministers, under President Nasry "Tito" Asfura, approved the executive decree the night of July 16, 2026; it was published the next day as Decreto Ejecutivo No. PCM-014-2026 in La Gaceta No. 37,196 (July 17, 2026), citing ILO Conventions 29/105 and CAFTA-DR obligations. The decree (Art. 4) prohibits importing goods produced wholly or partly with forced/compulsory labor, takes effect on publication, and directs Customs to build the prohibited-goods list into its risk-management system (Art. 7: intercepted goods face re-export or destruction at importer cost). Per the decree's own text, the Labour Ministry's implementing ministerial agreement carrying the specific prohibited-goods list is due within 30 days of entry into force, i.e. around August 15-16, 2026; re-checked August 4, 2026 and neither the list nor the implementing regulations have yet been published -- a near-term watch item. Source: Official USTR hearing transcript, Day 1, July 7, 2026; La Gaceta (official gazette) No. 37,196, July 17, 2026, via leyes.hn. USTR issued its FINAL Section 301 forced-labor determination on July 23, 2026 (Ambassador Greer, per direction of the President), confirming a final tariff of 10% for Honduras, timed to replace the expiring Section 122 10% global surcharge. Source: USTR press release and White House presidential action, July 23, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (Decreto Ejecutivo PCM-014-2026, published in La Gaceta No. 37,196, July 17, 2026; effective on publication, with the Labour Ministry's prohibited-goods list and implementing regulations due ~Aug 15-16, 2026 and still unpublished as of Aug 4)

Summary and Source: The U.S.-Jordan Agreement on Reciprocal Trade, signed July 21, 2026, commits Jordan under Article 2.9(1) -- text directly verified -- to prohibit importation of goods mined, produced or manufactured wholly or in part by forced or compulsory labor within five years of entry into force, and to recognize and presumptively enforce US Section 307 Withhold Release Order determinations. RESOLVED this run: the 10% tariff figure, previously carried as sourced only to Law360 and unverified against the agreement's Annex I, is now confirmed from the primary US source -- USTR's Federal Register notice (doc 2026-15181, published July 28, 2026) states the Trade Representative determined, "including consideration of Jordan's commitment in its ART related to prohibiting the importation of forced labor goods," to "impose 10 percent tariffs on products of Jordan, except as provided in Annex I and Annex II, Parts A, N, and O." Summary and Source: Malaysia's 10% tier rests on its US Agreement on Reciprocal Trade (signed October 2025), which Minister Johari Abdul Ghani confirmed on July 25, 2026 is signed but not ratified -- the 2-year clock to legislate a forced-labour import ban starts only on ratification. Malay-language sources (Utusan Malaysia, RTM) add that Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has said the US has not yet submitted a tariff proposal for ratification, so the matter remains pending on the US side as well. The earlier "null and void" episode followed the February 20, 2026 US Supreme Court ruling striking down IEEPA-based reciprocal tariffs and has since been superseded; that ruling does not disturb this action, since USTR's Federal Register notice rests solely on Sections 301(b) and 304(a) of the Trade Act of 1974 and never invokes IEEPA (verified directly against the notice). No forced-labour import-ban bill has been tabled. Source: Malay Mail and New Straits Times, July 25, 2026; Utusan Malaysia and RTM; Federal Register doc 2026-15181.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Partial (US-Malaysia Agreement on Reciprocal Trade signed October 2025, still NOT ratified as of August 1, 2026; the 2-year clock to enact a domestic forced-labour import ban begins only on ratification, and no domestic bill has been tabled)

Summary and Source: Mexico's forced-labor import ban derives from a Ministry of Economy regulation implementing USMCA Article 23.6, published in the Diario Oficial de la Federacion on February 17, 2023 and effective May 2023, administered with the Labour Ministry (STPS); USTR credits it but assesses enforcement as weak, placing Mexico in the 10% tier. The 45-day consultation on non-USMCA-covered trade has concluded, with Economy Minister Ebrard confirming the 10% Section 301 rate substitutes for, rather than stacks on, the expired Section 122 surcharge, leaving Mexico's effective burden unchanged; USMCA-compliant goods (~85% of exports) remain exempt. Flagged for the tracker but OUTSIDE its scope: Ebrard has warned of a separate pending Section 301 "excess manufacturing capacity" investigation covering 16 economies that could bring fresh tariffs as early as August 2026 -- unrelated to forced labor and not tracked here. Source: Diario Oficial de la Federacion, February 17, 2023; Mexico Business News, July 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (Ministry of Economy regulation implementing USMCA Article 23.6, published in the Diario Oficial February 17, 2023, effective May 2023; USTR assesses enforcement as weak)

Summary and Source: New Zealand rejects USTR's findings -- Prime Minister Christopher Luxon called the 12.5% tariff "extremely disappointing" and said the investigation "did not provide meaningful evidence" of forced labour, and Trade Minister Todd McClay called the process "not rigorous" while confirming NZ will not retaliate. NZ has no forced-labour import prohibition: only a narrow prison-labour import ban under section 96 of the Customs and Excise Act 2018, which provides a pathway for a broader ban that has never been exercised. The Modern Slavery Bill is a disclosure regime rather than an import ban and remains with the Education and Workforce Select Committee, due to report back August 31, 2026; with a general election set for October 1, 2026 it is unlikely to reach a second reading before dissolution. Source: RNZ and Interest.co.nz, July 2026; MFAT; DLA Piper; Transparency International NZ.

Summary and Source: Nicaragua enacted Ley No. 1280 (published in La Gaceta, April 9, 2026), adding Article 16 Bis to the customs self-clearance law (Ley No. 265), requiring importers, free-zone operators, and temporary-admission regimes to submit a sworn declaration that goods were not produced wholly or partly with forced labor, per an official format set by Customs Directorate Circular CT-027-2026; customs (DGA) may demand supply-chain traceability documentation and refer falsification for prosecution. This is a genuine enacted customs-law provision, but it establishes a declaration/investigation regime rather than an outright import prohibition, so it is classified Partial. Source: EY tax alert; Garcia & Bodan law firm summary, 2026.

Summary and Source: On July 21, 2026 -- two days before USTR's final determination -- Norway's Ministry of Trade, Industry and Fisheries announced a trade ban on products made with forced labour. Trade Minister Cecilie Myrseth: "Tvangsarbeid er selvfolgelig forbudt i Norge i dag, og gjennom dette regelverket innforer vi ogsa et forbud mot import av varer fremstilt ved tvangsarbeid" ("Forced labour is of course already prohibited in Norway today, and through this framework we are also introducing a ban on importing goods made with forced labour"). It covers import, export and sale, and is implemented by incorporating EU Regulation 2024/3015 (marked "Text with EEA relevance") into Norwegian law via the EEA Agreement, in force no later than December 14, 2027; the government committed to that date even if EEA incorporation runs late. As of this run no lovforslag/Proposition has been tabled to the Storting and no Norwegian implementing instrument has been enacted (an earlier hoering on the EU proposal closed with 26 responses), so this remains a government decision rather than an in-force ban. regjeringen.no returns HTTP 403 to automated fetching, so its text has not been read directly; content is confirmed via NRK, NTB and adressa.no. Separately, Norway called the 12.5% tariff unjustified and has requested WTO dispute-settlement consultations. Source: regjeringen.no press release, reported by NRK July 21, 2026 19:41 and wired by NTB July 22, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Partial (formal Norwegian government decision announced July 21, 2026 to ban import/export/sale of forced-labour-produced goods by incorporating EU Regulation 2024/3015 via the EEA Agreement, in force no later than December 14, 2027; no Storting proposition tabled and no Norwegian implementing instrument enacted yet)

Summary and Source: Peru's forced-labour import-ban bill was formally submitted to Congress on July 2, 2026 with "very urgent" status requested, and referred to the Foreign Trade and Economy committees on July 6, but was never taken up: the Foreign Trade Commission closed its 2025-2026 session without addressing it and the Permanent Commission's term ended July 15. NEW this run: Foreign Trade and Tourism Minister Rogers Valencia said the Executive is folding a forced-labour import prohibition -- barring dealings with companies that use forced labour -- into its formal request to the new Congress for delegated legislative powers ("facultades legislativas"), with the Council of Ministers due to consider the request on August 5, 2026. That is a second, faster route than the stalled bill, but as of this run it is a request for powers rather than a published measure, so it does not by itself change the classification. The Lima Chamber of Commerce continues to urge Congress to prioritise the bill. Source: Congreso del Peru communications; Gestion and La Republica, August 3, 2026; RPP Noticias, July 24, 2026; Infobae.

On review this is a domestic labor-enforcement/licensing measure, not a bill establishing a prohibition on *importing* forced-labor-made goods, so it does not meet the bar for Partial under the standing classification policy; reverted to No. Source: Korea JoongAng Daily, July 9-10, 2026; Newsworker/Newsfreezone (Korean), Hankyung, July 15, 2026. Summary and Source: Switzerland disputes USTR's findings, maintaining that existing constitutional, civil and criminal law suffices; swissinfo.ch notes that unlike the EU, Switzerland has no legislation explicitly prohibiting forced-labour imports, which is the stated basis for its higher tier, and that a draft due-diligence law would reach only around 30 large companies rather than banning imports. New this run: Switzerland concluded a broader US trade agreement lowering its general tariff to about 15% in exchange for roughly $200bn of US investment through 2028. Checked specifically for a forced-labour or Section 307 clause per the Jordan precedent -- this is a general tariff-and-investment deal with no forced-labour import-prohibition commitment found, so it does not place Switzerland on the RTA-commitment watchlist. Source: swissinfo.ch, July 24, 2026; Barchart/Reuters, July 2026.

Summary and Source: Taiwan's 10%-tier eligibility rests on its February 12, 2026 US Agreement on Reciprocal Trade, under which Taiwan committed to prohibit forced-labor-produced imports. This is administrative machinery rather than a statutory prohibition: no bill has been formally introduced in the Legislative Yuan, and the separate Employment Service Act amendments remain in preparation. Classified Partial on the same reasoning applied to the Philippines' Joint Administrative Order -- an enforcement mechanism under existing law is not itself an enacted import ban. Source: Taipei Times, July 31, 2026; Focus Taiwan, June 2026; USTR fact sheet, February 2026.

Summary and Source: The specific domestic instrument has now been located and verified directly: Trinidad and Tobago's Finance Act, 2026 (Act No. 16 of 2026), assented to on 25 June 2026 and published in Legal Supplement Part A to the Trinidad and Tobago Gazette, Vol. 65, No. 111, 29 June 2026, section 24 amends the Customs Act (Chap. 78:01) section 45(1) by inserting a new paragraph: "(w) all goods produced from forced labour as designated by the Minister with responsibility for trade". Section 45(1) is the Customs Act's list of prohibited/restricted imports, so this is a genuine, enacted, gazetted forced-labor import prohibition (designation-dependent -- the specific list of goods is left to the Minister with responsibility for trade to designate, similar in structure to several other economies' framework-style bans). This confirms and supersedes the prior entry's reliance on USTR's Federal Register final-action notice (which had stated, without naming the instrument, that Trinidad and Tobago "adopt[ed] a forced labor import prohibition subsequent to the publication of the June 5, 2026 FRN" -- the Finance Act's 25 June 2026 assent date fits neatly within that window). USTR's final action (July 23, 2026) placed Trinidad and Tobago in the 10% tariff tier on this basis. Source: Trinidad and Tobago e-Gazette (printery.gov.tt), Finance Act 2026 (Act No. 16 of 2026), 29 June 2026; USTR Federal Register final-action notice, July 23, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (Finance Act, 2026, Act No. 16 of 2026, assented 25 June 2026, gazetted 29 June 2026, section 24 amends Customs Act Chap. 78:01 s.45(1) by adding paragraph (w) prohibiting the importation of goods produced from forced labour, as designated by the Minister with responsibility for trade -- a framework-style ban pending ministerial designation of the specific goods list)
